sections.title: How does the Mixed liquor volatile suspended solids calculator work?
sections.html:
The Mixed liquor volatile suspended solids calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports average untreated in-fluent COD in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the method); then you type in the sample volume (Mixed liquor suspended solid experiment), the weight of filter paper, the MLSS and the sample volume (Fixed solids experiment).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Mixed liquor volatile suspended solids calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Average untreated in-fluent COD=average primary treated COD + primary effluent COD
Primary effluent COD=(50000 ÷ 417) × COD added to aeration ÷ flow
Free-board=-25 ÷ 187 × aeration volume ÷ (length × width) + sidewall depth
Aeration volume=(1 ÷ 24) × HRT × flow
MLVSS (mass)=COD added to aeration ÷ F ÷ M ratio
MLVSS (mass)=(417 ÷ 50000000) × MLVSS (conc.) × aeration volume

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Method set to Laboratory, Average primary treated COD = 10 g/L and Primary effluent COD = 10 g/L. Working through the relationship above gives Average untreated in-fluent COD = 20 g/L.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Average untreated in-fluent COD = 20 g/L should be roughly the size you expected from Method set to Laboratory and Average primary treated COD = 10 g/L.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Volume, opening in cubic decimeters
  • Mass, opening in grams
  • Mass, opening in grams
  • Density, opening in grams per liter
  • Volume, opening in cubic decimeters
  • Mass, opening in grams

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Mixed liquor volatile suspended solids calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Putting a biological quantity into a scale you can picture
  • Supporting a lesson, a lecture or a field note
  • Comparing two organisms, populations or processes
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the sample volume, the weight of filter paper and the MLSS — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Mixed liquor volatile suspended solids calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns average untreated in-fluent COD, derived from the sample volume, the weight of filter paper and the MLSS. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Mixed liquor volatile suspended solids calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the sample volume, the weight of filter paper and the MLSS, which is 14 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter sample volume (Mixed liquor suspended solid experiment) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Sample volume (Mixed liquor suspended solid experiment) opens in cubic decimeters and the chip beside it offers 40 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Average untreated in-fluent COD = 20 g/L. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Mixed liquor volatile suspended solids calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
